note: Keep them if you set it before yourself that they can be kept: ability tracks the set will. Commandments easy to the willing heart.
Rewards by worth of deeds; the same man turning to opposites proves power by free deliberate choice. The classic anti-fate argument.
Evil completed by freedom of deliberate choice; the wicked wicked through himself, by the self-determining power given from God.
Virtue and vice by own choice in men and angels alike: honor and punishment presuppose power.
God made man free and self-determining; the one who wants to can procure eternal life. Obedience unto life as disobedience unto death.
The ancient law of human liberty: counsel, not force. Power of choice in man as in angels, so obedience merits the good.
In our power to present ourselves for training and obey; refusal wrongs our own soul.
Law proves liberty: no law binds one lacking owed obedience in his own power. Full freedom toward either side.
Rational beings judge impressions and choose; praise and blame track the use of reason, not outside causes.
The first man made self-determining, the race inheriting the same freedom: authority to obey whatever he wills.

Lactantius argues God permits error and impiety so that judgment stays just, which is meaningful only if people genuinely could choose otherwise. His wider work, notably On the Wrath of God, defends human free will outright.
Servants ruined as they forget commandments and walk in deceits: personal turning, personal ruin.
Not made to die: we die through ourselves. Self-determining power ruined us, and the ruined can refuse again.
The tree not evil; disobedience evil. Adam the child overreached, and disobedience brought death.

Rashness from Adam brings condemnation and death, yet repentance stands open and covenanted. Note the other side: On the Soul 40 to 41 teaches a transmitted taint too, and both Tertullian rows sit on the timeline.
Hand him faith and subjection, and receive his perfecting art. Man offers, God completes: assistance, not coercion.
Building and watching still ours, yet vain without the Lord who completes. Willing and running need the mercy that crowns them.

Counsel, works, and faith alike preserve free decision: according to your faith be it done to you.
Caution: Julian here quotes the view he attacks, branding its holders Manichaeans. His affirmation lies in the refutation: a lost will forcing all to sin is the error he rejects.
Caution: opponent-quotation. Julian cites the lost-will, flesh-necessity doctrine to condemn it as Manichaean impiety, not to profess it.
His own argument: if sin were inborn from the first birth it could neither condemn marriage justly nor ever be removed from infants.
Reductio: sin inherited through nature makes nature itself diabolical and forfeits the image of God.
No sin without will, no will without developed freedom: infants without reason have no sin whatsoever.
Julian frames the dilemma both sides press, grace or will, and promises the ungodliness exposed: he defends will and grace together, denying neither.
Five syllogisms against birth-sin, preserved in Augustine recap of the Julian side: Creator, marriage, baptism, justice, and capable nature each exclude it.

Re-pointed 2026-09-28: the old section stated only the letter purpose and said nothing about grace. Julian here confesses grace necessary and healing, working according to the capacity of those who approach: aid to an acting will, his constant position against Augustine.
